quick: Usually 50-150 mg/day; typically 50 mg morning + 100 mg evening (range 50-300 mg/day)
Take with liquid; may be taken with or without food
Avoid unless clearly necessary; safety not established
Avoid; expected to pass into breast milk

summary: Opipramol is a tricyclic-structured agent used mainly in Europe (e.g., Germany - Insidon) for generalized anxiety disorder and somatoform disorders. Unlike classic tricyclic antidepressants it does not appreciably inhibit monoamine reuptake; its action is attributed to high-affinity binding at sigma-1 and sigma-2 receptors plus histamine H1 antagonism, giving an anxiolytic and mild antidepressant/sedative profile. It is NOT FDA-approved.
indications: Adjunctive treatment of anxiety/restlessness and associated depressive symptoms (per EU/SmPC labelling)

dosage.d: 50-150 mg/day; commonly 50 mg in morning/midday plus 100 mg in evening
dosage.t: In divided doses, larger dose at night due to sedation
dosage.n: Range up to 300 mg/day; titrate gradually; reduce in elderly
Lower doses due to increased sensitivity and reduced clearance

admin: Take the larger dose in the evening because of sedative effect
Titrate gradually and taper when stopping to avoid discontinuation symptoms
Use lower doses in the elderly and in hepatic/renal impairment
moa: Opipramol does not significantly inhibit reuptake of noradrenaline or serotonin (unlike classic tricyclic antidepressants). Its anxiolytic and mood-stabilising effects are attributed to high-affinity binding at sigma-1 and sigma-2 receptors, together with antagonism at histamine H1 receptors (and some dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2 affinity), producing anxiolytic, sedative and mild antidepressant effects.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to opipramol or other tricyclic agents
Acute intoxication with alcohol, hypnotics, analgesics or psychotropic drugs
Recent myocardial infarction / acute cardiac conduction disorders
Concurrent MAO inhibitor use (and within ~14 days)
monitor: Blood counts and liver function on prolonged therapy

preg: Safety in pregnancy is not established; avoid unless clearly necessary, particularly in the first trimester and near term. Follow EU SmPC guidance.
lact: Opipramol is expected to pass into breast milk; breastfeeding is generally not recommended during treatment.
renal: Use with caution and consider dose reduction in significant renal impairment due to reduced elimination.
hepatic: Use with caution; reduce dose or avoid in significant hepatic impairment as the drug is hepatically metabolized.

major: MAO inhibitors - risk of serotonergic/hypertensive crisis (contraindicated; observe washout)
Other QT-prolonging drugs - additive arrhythmia risk
CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, hypnotics) - additive sedation/respiratory depression
moderate: Antihypertensives (e.g., clonidine/guanethidine) - effects may be altered
CYP2D6 inhibitors - may raise opipramol levels
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive CNS depression and sedation
interactions.diagnostics: ECG (QT), liver function tests and blood counts on long-term therapy

monitoring: ECG/QT interval where cardiac risk factors are present
Liver function tests and complete blood count on long-term use
Mental status and degree of sedation, especially in the elderly
counsel: Sedation is common at first - take the larger dose at night and avoid driving until you know how it affects you
Avoid alcohol and other sedating medicines
Do not stop abruptly - taper under guidance to avoid withdrawal symptoms
Report fainting, palpitations, fever/sore throat, or yellowing of skin/eyes
Tell your doctor about all other medicines, especially MAO inhibitors
pk: Anxiolytic/sedative effect within days; full anxiolytic effect over 1-2 weeks
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: NOT FDA-approved; this record is based on EU/SmPC (e.g., Insidon) and BNF/secondary references rather than an FDA label.
Despite its tricyclic structure, opipramol is essentially NOT a monoamine-reuptake inhibitor - its anxiolytic effect comes from sigma-receptor and H1 activity.
It still carries classic tricyclic-type cautions: anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, QT prolongation, seizure-threshold lowering, and dangerous overdose toxicity.
Avoid combining with MAO inhibitors and observe an appropriate washout period.
missed: Take the missed dose when remembered unless it is close to the next dose, in which case skip it. Do not double up. Because of sedation, generally do not take a missed daytime dose late in the day.
overdose: Tricyclic-type overdose can be life-threatening: anticholinergic toxidrome, CNS depression/coma, seizures, and cardiotoxicity (QRS widening, arrhythmia, hypotension). Management is supportive with cardiac monitoring; sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening/arrhythmia, benzodiazepines for seizures, and intensive supportive care. Contact poison control.
